opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that prompting is a fantastic starting point, but it eventually hits a ceiling. Most AI engineers today build applications by stitching together prompts, maybe adding some retrieval, maybe some tool calls, and that gets you surprisingly far. But at some point you're fighting the model. You keep adding instructions, examples, edge cases, and the prompt turns into a giant, fragile document that breaks whenever the underlying model changes.

Training, whether that's fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or distillation into a smaller model, lets you actually change the model's behavior instead of just asking nicely. You can bake in the domain knowledge, the output format, the reasoning style your application needs. Often you end up with something smaller, cheaper, faster, and more reliable than a frontier model with a huge prompt.

The problem is that training has historically been the domain of ML researchers. You need to know how to curate data, set up infrastructure, pick hyperparameters, run evaluations, and none of that is how most application developers think. So there's a big gap. The people closest to the problem, who know what good outputs look like and what their users need, aren't the ones who can train models.

What I want is to close that gap. If we give AI engineers tools that make training feel as approachable as writing a prompt, where they describe what they want, generate or curate data, and get a specialized model out the other end, then a lot more people can build things that actually work in production. I think that's where a lot of the next wave of value comes from: not just better general models, but many specialized models built by the people who understand the use cases best.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts specialized models with frontier models, but does not clearly say this reduces dependence on frontier providers.

r002.rationale: It says training can produce a model that is “smaller, cheaper” than a frontier model with a huge prompt.

r003.rationale: It says training can bake in the domain knowledge, output format, and reasoning style an application needs, making models more reliable for those uses.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core of why we started Bespoke Labs. If you look at where most AI engineers are today, they're building on top of closed models through an API, and the main lever they have is the prompt. And prompting is great, it gets you really far, really fast. But at some point you hit a ceiling. You're stuffing more and more examples into the context, you're adding retries, you're adding guardrails, and the cost and latency go up while the accuracy kind of plateaus. And the frustrating thing is that the engineer usually knows exactly what's going wrong. They have the failure cases sitting right there in their logs. They just don't have a way to push that knowledge back into the model.

So the thing we kept seeing, both from my time at Google and then talking to teams building products, is that the people who can fine-tune or do RL on a model are a pretty small group. It's a handful of research labs and a few well-resourced ML teams. The actual AI engineers, the ones shipping the application and who understand the task better than anyone, mostly don't have access to that. Not because it's intellectually out of reach, but because the tooling is painful. You need to curate data, you need infrastructure, you need to understand a bunch of hyperparameters, you need evals, and every piece of that is its own project.

And I think that's a historical accident more than anything. If you go back a few years, every ML engineer trained models. That was the job. Then the big pretrained models arrived and training got concentrated into the labs, and everyone else moved to prompting. Which was the right move at the time. But now the open models are really good, the techniques like distillation and RL with verifiable rewards have matured, and the gap between "I can write a prompt" and "I can shape this model's behavior" shouldn't be as big as it is.

What we want is for training to feel like just another tool in the engineer's workflow. You have your task, you have examples of what good looks like, maybe you have a verifier or a reward signal, and you should be able to go from that to a smaller, faster, more accurate model without having to become a research scientist. Because when the application engineer can do that loop themselves, they iterate way faster than if they have to throw it over the wall to a separate team. They own the data, they own the evals, they own the model.

So for me the motivation is partly economic, you get cheaper and more reliable systems, and partly about who gets to participate. I'd rather have a hundred thousand engineers who can specialize models for their domain than a few hundred people at a few companies deciding what the models are good at.

r001.rationale: It contrasts reliance on closed-model APIs with training models around engineers’ own tasks, then says they should be able to produce and own a specialized model. This clearly presents training as a way to rely less on closed providers.

r002.rationale: It says the motivation is economic and that engineers can get “cheaper” systems by training models for their tasks.

r003.rationale: It says task-specific training can produce a “more accurate” model and that it can improve accuracy where prompting has plateaued.

astra-6.text:
Because prompting is a great place to start, but it shouldn’t be the only tool available to you. You can get a prototype working very quickly, and then you start seeing cases where the model doesn’t quite do what you want. You add more instructions, more examples, and at some point you’re spending a lot of effort managing that prompt.

If you have examples of what good behavior looks like, you should be able to use those to improve the model directly. That shouldn’t require becoming an expert in distributed training or knowing how to manage GPUs. An AI engineer should be able to take their data, train a model, evaluate whether it actually improved, and iterate.

And it’s not that training replaces prompting. They’re complementary. The goal is to give engineers more ways to solve the problem, including potentially using a smaller, faster model that’s better suited to their particular task.

r001.rationale: It mentions using a smaller model suited to a task, but does not say this reduces dependence on frontier providers such as OpenAI.

r002.rationale: It describes a potentially smaller, faster model but does not state that training for a specific use reduces AI costs.

r003.rationale: It says examples of desired behavior can be used to improve the model directly and describes tailoring a model to a particular task.

sol-6.1.text:
Prompting makes it really easy to get started. You can take a model, give it instructions and a few examples, and build something useful. But as you iterate, you may find that the prompt gets longer and longer, and you’re still struggling to get consistent behavior. At that point, you should have access to another tool: training the model on examples of what you actually want.

I don’t think an AI engineer should need to become a researcher to do that. They already understand their application and can often recognize a good response versus a bad one. We want to make it easier to turn that knowledge into data, train a model, and evaluate whether it’s actually better. Prompting and training are complementary ways to improve a system, and engineers should be able to move between them as their application needs change.

r001.rationale: The response recommends training on application-specific examples but does not say this reduces dependence on frontier providers.

r002.rationale: It does not mention reducing AI costs.

r003.rationale: It presents training on examples of desired behavior as a way to improve an application and evaluate whether the model is better for that use.
